readerTitle: Why would a shop sell a $429 bread maker that nobody buys?
caseNote: 실제 연구 (Tversky & Kahneman 1974, Northcraft & Neale 1987) + 업계 일화 (Williams-Sonoma, 출처 불명확) + 가상 사례 (리노베이션 견적)
insight: 가격은 혼자 평가되지 않는다. 처음 본 숫자가 이후 모든 가격의 기준이 된다.

sources.text: Tversky & Kahneman (1974). Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases. Science.
Northcraft & Neale (1987). Experts, amateurs, and real estate. Org. Behavior and Human Decision Processes.
EU Price Indication Directive 98/6/EC, Art. 6a (Omnibus Directive 2019/2161 개정)
US FTC, Guides Against Deceptive Pricing (16 CFR Part 233)

factChecks.note: Williams-Sonoma 제빵기 일화는 마케팅 업계에서 널리 인용되지만 1차 출처가 불명확합니다. 카드에 "reportedly"를 남겨 두었고, 정식 출시 전에는 학술 사례로 바꾸는 것을 검토하세요.
Tversky & Kahneman 수치(25% / 45%)는 중앙값입니다. 문구에도 "median"을 명시했습니다.
규제 문구(EU 30일 최저가, FTC 가이드)는 국가별로 다릅니다. 출시 국가 기준으로 다시 확인해야 합니다.

cards.title: Why would a shop sell a $429 bread maker that nobody buys?
body: It sounds like a bad product decision. It might be the smartest one on the shelf.
In the next few minutes you'll make two pricing calls and learn the idea behind them.

image.label: Two bread makers on a shelf
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 매장 선반 위 제빵기 2대. 왼쪽의 큰 제품에 $429, 오른쪽의 작은 제품에 $279 가격표. 앱 목업과 같은 파스텔 톤에 부드러운 그림자.

cards.title: Your $279 bread maker isn't selling.
body: You run a kitchen store. Shoppers pick up the $279 model, turn it over, and put it back. Several tell you it feels expensive for a bread maker.
You can make one change this month. What do you try?

options.feedback: Sales may go up, but you just gave away $80 a unit, about 29% of the price. You also told shoppers the old price wasn't worth it. That's hard to undo.

options.text: Put a bigger $429 model right next to it
options.feedback: This is the move in a story marketers love to tell about Williams-Sonoma. The $429 model barely sold. Sales of the $279 model reportedly almost doubled. Next card: why.
Better information helps, but shoppers are still judging $279 against nothing. With no comparison, an unfamiliar price tends to feel high.

cards.title: The $429 model wasn't really for sale. It was for comparison.
body: Before, shoppers asked: *Is $279 a lot for a bread maker?* That's a hard question. Few people know what a bread maker should cost.
After, they asked: *Do I need the $429 one, or is $279 enough?* That's an easy question. Next to $429, $279 looks sensible.
The product didn't change. **The question in the shopper's head did.**

cards.title: Price anchoring
body: The first number people see becomes a **reference point**. Every price after it gets judged as higher or lower than that anchor, not on its own.
We're bad at judging absolute value (what's a fair price for a bread maker?) and good at judging relative value (is this more or less than that?). Anchors work in that gap.

image.label: Anchor at $429 → $279 feels lower
image.brief: 개념을 한 장으로 요약하는 인포그래픽. 위쪽에 닻 아이콘과 "$429", 아래쪽 화살표 끝에 "$279 feels reasonable". 텍스트는 최소화.

cards.title: Even a random number works.
body: In a 1974 study, Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman spun a wheel rigged to stop at either 10 or 65. Then they asked people what percentage of UN member countries were African.
People who saw 10 gave a median guess of 25%. People who saw 65 gave a median guess of 45%.
Everyone could see the wheel was random. It still moved their answers by 20 points.

image.label: Wheel of fortune stopping at 10 or 65
image.brief: 룰렛(행운의 바퀴)이 10과 65에 멈춘 두 컷을 나란히. 아래에 각각 "Guess: 25%" "Guess: 45%" 말풍선.

cards.title: Experts get anchored too.
body: In a 1987 study by Gregory Northcraft and Margaret Neale, real estate agents toured the same house and got the same information, except for the listing price.
Agents who were shown a higher listing price valued the house higher. Most of them said the listing price hadn't influenced them.
You'll find the same pattern on restaurant menus with one very expensive bottle of wine, and on software pricing pages that show the Enterprise plan first.

cards.title: A fake anchor is a liability.
body: "Was $300, now $199" works only if $300 was a real price. Customers who spot an invented reference price stop trusting every other number you show them.
It can also be illegal. In the EU, a price-cut claim has to refer to the lowest price of the previous 30 days. In the US, the FTC has guidance against fictitious former prices.
Good anchors are **real options**: products someone could actually buy.

cards.title: Now it's a renovation quote.
body: You run a kitchen-renovation company. You give homeowners one quote: $18,000. Many say it's more than they expected and stop replying.
Which change uses anchoring honestly?

options.text: Quote three real options: $12,000, $18,000 and $32,000, starting with the $32,000 one
options.feedback: Right. Each option is a job you'd really do. Next to $32,000, $18,000 looks sensible, and some clients will choose the premium job.
If it was never $24,000, this is a fictitious reference price. Homeowners compare quotes, and a fake discount can cost you trust and possibly a legal problem.

options.text: Add "Our most popular choice" to the quote
options.feedback: This can help, but it's social proof, a different lever. Nothing changed about what $18,000 gets compared to.

cards.title: Never let a price stand alone.
body: Decide what your customer compares you to before they decide for themselves.
**Try it today:** open your price list, quote or menu. What's the first number a customer sees? Is it working for you?
